nodes.label: God / Yahweh
nodes.description: God is presented as creator of the heavens and earth and as the one who addresses Noah about the flood and covenant. The narrative also uses the name Yahweh God.
nodes.editorial_note: Narrative referent within this pilot only; no theological identity links. Possessive compounds God’s Spirit and God’s sons are not distinct mentions of those concepts here.

nodes.label: Adam
nodes.description: Adam is named as Eve’s husband and Seth’s father in the early family narrative. This individual is kept distinct from the collective use of “Adam” for humankind in Genesis 5:2.
nodes.editorial_note: Generic man and collective Adam in 5:2 intentionally excluded.

nodes.label: Eve
nodes.description: Eve is the name the man gives his wife; she later gives birth to Cain and Abel. Her name is explained in the narrative in connection with being the mother of all the living.
nodes.editorial_note: woman/wife coreference omitted from mention layer.

nodes.label: Cain
nodes.description: Cain, born to Eve, tills the ground and brings an offering to Yahweh. He kills his brother Abel and later lives in Nod, east of Eden.

nodes.label: Abel
nodes.description: Abel is Cain’s brother and a keeper of sheep whose offering Yahweh regards favorably. Cain kills him in the field.

nodes.label: Seth
nodes.description: Seth is the son named after Abel’s death and the father of Enosh. Genesis 5 continues Adam’s genealogy through him.

nodes.label: Enosh
nodes.description: Enosh is Seth’s son and Kenan’s father in the Genesis 5 genealogy. The account of his naming also notes that people began to call on Yahweh’s name at that time.

nodes.label: Enoch (Cain’s son)
nodes.description: This Enoch is Cain’s son and Irad’s father; Cain names a city after him. He is distinct from Enoch, Jared’s son, in Genesis 5.

nodes.label: Irad
nodes.description: Irad is Enoch’s son and Mehujael’s father in the genealogy descending from Cain. The passage provides no further individual story about him.

nodes.label: Mehujael
nodes.description: Mehujael is Irad’s son and Methushael’s father in Cain’s family line. He appears in the compact genealogy leading to Lamech.

nodes.label: Methushael
nodes.description: Methushael is Mehujael’s son and the father of the Lamech in Cain’s line. He is not the similarly named Methuselah in Genesis 5.

nodes.label: Lamech (Cain line)
nodes.description: This Lamech, a descendant of Cain, takes Adah and Zillah as wives. He tells them that he has killed a man; he is distinct from Noah’s father, also named Lamech.

nodes.label: Adah
nodes.description: Adah is one of Lamech’s two wives in Cain’s family line and the mother of Jabal. Lamech addresses her and Zillah in his speech about killing a man.

nodes.label: Zillah
nodes.description: Zillah is one of Lamech’s two wives in Cain’s family line and the mother of Tubal Cain. She and Adah are addressed in Lamech’s speech.

nodes.label: Jabal
nodes.description: Jabal is Adah’s son and Jubal’s brother. The text describes him as the father of those who live in tents and keep livestock.

nodes.label: Jubal
nodes.description: Jubal is Jabal’s brother and is described as the father of all who play the harp and pipe. His brief notice appears in Cain’s family genealogy.

nodes.label: Tubal Cain
nodes.description: Tubal Cain is Zillah’s son, described as a forger of cutting tools of bronze and iron. Naamah is named as his sister.

nodes.label: Naamah
nodes.description: Naamah is named as Tubal Cain’s sister in Cain’s family genealogy. This passage gives no further individual story about her.

nodes.label: Kenan
nodes.description: Kenan is Enosh’s son and Mahalalel’s father in the Genesis 5 genealogy. His entry records his lifespan and other unnamed children.

nodes.label: Mahalalel
nodes.description: Mahalalel is Kenan’s son and Jared’s father in the Genesis 5 genealogy. His entry records his lifespan and other unnamed children.

nodes.label: Jared
nodes.description: Jared is Mahalalel’s son and the father of the Enoch in Genesis 5. This identifies a different Enoch from Cain’s son in Genesis 4.

nodes.label: Enoch (Jared’s son)
nodes.description: This Enoch is Jared’s son and Methuselah’s father. The narrative says that he walked with God and was not found because God took him; he is distinct from Cain’s son Enoch.

nodes.label: Methuselah
nodes.description: Methuselah is Enoch’s son and the father of Noah’s father Lamech. His entry records a lifespan of 969 years within the narrative’s genealogy.

nodes.label: Lamech (Noah’s father)
nodes.description: This Lamech is Methuselah’s son and Noah’s father, not the Lamech in Cain’s line. On naming Noah, he speaks of hoped-for comfort from the toil associated with the cursed ground.

nodes.label: Noah
nodes.description: Noah is presented as a righteous man who follows God’s instructions concerning the ship and survives the flood with his family. God later addresses him and his sons about the covenant.

nodes.label: Shem
nodes.description: Shem is one of Noah’s three sons and enters the ship with the family. He and Japheth cover their father without looking at his nakedness, and Genesis 11 traces a genealogy from Shem through Arpachshad.

nodes.label: Ham
nodes.description: Ham is one of Noah’s three sons and is identified as Canaan’s father. He sees his father’s nakedness and tells his brothers; the subsequent curse spoken by Noah names Canaan, not Ham.

nodes.label: Japheth
nodes.description: Japheth is one of Noah’s three sons who enter the ship. He and Shem cover their father without looking at his nakedness, and Genesis 10 lists his sons.

nodes.label: Nimrod
nodes.description: Nimrod is presented as Cush’s offspring and a mighty hunter before Yahweh. The beginning of his kingdom includes Babel, Erech, Accad and Calneh in Shinar.

nodes.label: Arpachshad
nodes.description: Arpachshad is Shem’s son and Shelah’s father. He appears in both the Genesis 10 family list and the genealogy leading toward Terah’s family in Genesis 11.

nodes.label: Shelah
nodes.description: Shelah is Arpachshad’s son and Eber’s father. His place in the family line is repeated in Genesis 10 and 11.

nodes.label: Eber
nodes.description: Eber is Shelah’s son and the father of Peleg and Joktan. Genesis 11 follows the branch through Peleg.

nodes.label: Peleg
nodes.description: Peleg is Eber’s son, Joktan’s brother and Reu’s father. The account connects his name with the statement that the earth was divided in his days.

nodes.label: Reu
nodes.description: Reu is Peleg’s son and Serug’s father in the genealogy from Shem toward Terah. His entry also records years lived and other unnamed children.

nodes.label: Serug
nodes.description: Serug is Reu’s son and the father of the older Nahor in Genesis 11. This Nahor is Terah’s father, not Terah’s son of the same name.

nodes.label: Nahor (Serug’s son)
nodes.description: This Nahor is Serug’s son and Terah’s father. He is distinct from Terah’s son Nahor, who marries Milcah.

nodes.label: Terah
nodes.description: Terah is the father of Abram, Nahor and Haran. He leaves Ur of the Chaldees with Abram, Sarai and Lot toward Canaan, settles in Haran, and dies there.

nodes.label: Abraham (Abram)
nodes.description: Abram, renamed Abraham, travels to Canaan and is addressed by God about offspring and covenant. He is the father of Ishmael and Isaac, and after his death they bury him in the cave of Machpelah.

nodes.label: Nahor (Terah’s son)
nodes.description: This Nahor is Abraham’s brother, Milcah’s husband and Bethuel’s father. He is distinct from the older Nahor who is Terah’s father; the phrase “city of Nahor” is not resolved as a person mention here.

nodes.label: Haran (Terah’s son)
nodes.description: Haran is Terah’s son and the father of Lot, Milcah and Iscah. He dies in Ur of the Chaldees while Terah is still alive; he is not the place called Haran where the family later settles.

nodes.label: Lot
nodes.description: Lot is Haran’s son and Abraham’s nephew; he separates from Abraham and settles near Sodom. The account later describes his rescue from captivity and escape from Sodom to Zoar.

nodes.label: Sarah (Sarai)
nodes.description: Sarai, renamed Sarah, is Abraham’s wife and Isaac’s mother. She dies at Hebron and is buried by Abraham in the cave of Machpelah.

nodes.label: Milcah
nodes.description: Milcah is Nahor’s wife and Haran’s daughter. Later passages identify her as Bethuel’s mother and Rebekah’s grandmother.

nodes.label: Iscah
nodes.description: Iscah is named as a child of Haran in the notice about Abram’s and Nahor’s marriages. No further individual story is given here.

nodes.label: Eden
nodes.description: Eden is the region where Yahweh God plants the garden and places the man. A river is described as flowing out of Eden to water the garden; no modern location is established by this pilot.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual location only; no modern coordinates or geographic equivalence asserted.

nodes.label: Nod
nodes.description: Nod is the land east of Eden where Cain lives after leaving Yahweh’s presence. The pilot records this textual location without assigning modern coordinates.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual location only; no modern coordinates or geographic equivalence asserted.

nodes.label: Pishon
nodes.description: Pishon is the first named river in the account of the river flowing out of Eden. It is described as flowing through Havilah, a land associated with gold.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual location only; no modern coordinates or geographic equivalence asserted.

nodes.label: Gihon
nodes.description: Gihon is the second named river in the Eden river account. It is described as flowing through the whole land of Cush.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual location only; no modern coordinates or geographic equivalence asserted.

nodes.label: Hiddekel
nodes.description: Hiddekel is the third named river in the Eden river account. The text says it flows in front of Assyria; no modern-river identification is added here.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual location only; no modern coordinates or geographic equivalence asserted.

nodes.label: Euphrates
nodes.description: The Euphrates is the fourth named river in the Eden river account. This pilot records the name as given without reconstructing the river system’s geography.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual location only; no modern coordinates or geographic equivalence asserted.

nodes.label: Havilah (land)
nodes.description: Havilah is the land through which the Pishon flows, described as containing gold, bdellium and onyx. This place is not merged with the genealogical names Havilah elsewhere in Genesis 10.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual location only; no modern coordinates or geographic equivalence asserted.

nodes.label: Cush (land)
nodes.description: Cush is the land through which the Gihon is said to flow. This place entry is kept separate from Cush in the Genesis 10 genealogy, without asserting whether the names have a historical connection.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual location only; no modern coordinates or geographic equivalence asserted.

nodes.label: Assyria
nodes.description: Assyria is named in relation to Hiddekel and in the account of cities including Nineveh and Calah. This pilot does not resolve the actor in Genesis 10:11 or assign modern geographic boundaries.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual location only; no modern coordinates or geographic equivalence asserted.

nodes.label: Ararat’s mountains
nodes.description: Ararat’s mountains are where the ship comes to rest as the floodwaters recede. The phrase names a mountainous area in the text, not a uniquely identified modern summit.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual location only; no modern coordinates or geographic equivalence asserted.

nodes.label: Shinar
nodes.description: Shinar is the land containing the first cities named as part of Nimrod’s kingdom. The later Babel account places the travelers’ settlement on a plain in Shinar.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual location only; no modern coordinates or geographic equivalence asserted.

nodes.label: Babel
nodes.description: Babel is named among the beginnings of Nimrod’s kingdom and as the city associated with the confusion of language. These mentions share one editorial place entry here, without an archaeological identification.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual location only; no modern coordinates or geographic equivalence asserted.

nodes.label: Ur of the Chaldees
nodes.description: Ur of the Chaldees is named as Haran’s birthplace and the place where he dies. Terah’s household later leaves it to travel toward Canaan.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual location only; no modern coordinates or geographic equivalence asserted.

nodes.label: Canaan (land)
nodes.description: Canaan is the land Terah’s household intends to reach after leaving Ur of the Chaldees. The party instead settles in Haran in this passage; this land entry is separate from Canaan in Noah’s family genealogy.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual location only; no modern coordinates or geographic equivalence asserted.

nodes.label: Haran (place)
nodes.description: Haran is the place where Terah’s traveling household settles on the way toward Canaan and where Terah dies. It is distinct from Terah’s son Haran, who had died in Ur of the Chaldees.

nodes.label: Serpent in Eden
nodes.description: The serpent questions the woman about God’s command and tells her that eating will not bring the death she describes. The Genesis account presents a speaking animal; this pilot does not equate it with a later named figure.
nodes.editorial_note: No equation with Satan or another entity.

nodes.label: Noah’s ship
nodes.description: The ship is the vessel God instructs Noah to make to preserve life through the flood. It carries Noah, his family and animals, then comes to rest on Ararat’s mountains.
nodes.editorial_note: WEB uses ship, not ark. Noah’s ship is a display label, not an asserted source alias.

nodes.label: Tree of life
nodes.description: The tree of life is named among the trees in the garden. After the man is sent out, cherubim and a flaming sword guard the way to it.

nodes.label: Tree of the knowledge of good and evil
nodes.description: The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is named among the garden’s trees. God commands the man not to eat from it and warns that eating will bring death.

nodes.label: Canaan
nodes.description: Canaan is presented as Ham’s offspring and becomes the target of Noah’s spoken curse. Genesis 10 lists descendants and peoples under this name; this entry leaves individual and people-group readings unresolved.
nodes.editorial_note: Genealogical presentation in the text; individual/eponym/people interpretation is not resolved.

nodes.label: Cush
nodes.description: Cush is listed among Ham’s sons and as the parent of Nimrod, alongside other genealogical descendants. This entry preserves the family-list presentation without equating it with the land called Cush.
nodes.editorial_note: Genealogical presentation in the text; individual/eponym/people interpretation is not resolved.

nodes.label: Mizraim
nodes.description: Mizraim is listed among Ham’s sons and as the ancestor of several named groups in Genesis 10. The entry preserves that genealogical presentation without deciding between individual and people-group readings.
nodes.editorial_note: Genealogical presentation in the text; individual/eponym/people interpretation is not resolved.

nodes.label: Put
nodes.description: Put is one of the sons listed under Ham in Genesis 10. This brief genealogical entry does not supply an individual story or resolve whether the name represents a person or people.
nodes.editorial_note: Genealogical presentation in the text; individual/eponym/people interpretation is not resolved.

nodes.label: Gomer
nodes.description: Gomer is listed among Japheth’s sons and as the parent of Ashkenaz, Riphath and Togarmah. This pilot retains the genealogy’s wording without forcing an individual or people-group interpretation.
nodes.editorial_note: Genealogical presentation in the text; individual/eponym/people interpretation is not resolved.

nodes.label: Magog
nodes.description: Magog is one of the sons listed under Japheth in Genesis 10. No later uses of the name or modern people-group identifications are attached to this pilot entry.
nodes.editorial_note: Genealogical presentation in the text; individual/eponym/people interpretation is not resolved.

nodes.label: Madai
nodes.description: Madai is one of the sons listed under Japheth in Genesis 10. The entry preserves its place in that genealogy without adding a modern ethnic or geographic identification.
nodes.editorial_note: Genealogical presentation in the text; individual/eponym/people interpretation is not resolved.

nodes.label: Javan
nodes.description: Javan is listed among Japheth’s sons and as the parent of Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim and Dodanim. The pilot leaves the individual or people-group interpretation unresolved.
nodes.editorial_note: Genealogical presentation in the text; individual/eponym/people interpretation is not resolved.

nodes.label: Tubal
nodes.description: Tubal is one of the sons listed under Japheth in Genesis 10. This genealogical name is distinct from the earlier craftsman named Tubal Cain.
nodes.editorial_note: Genealogical presentation in the text; individual/eponym/people interpretation is not resolved.

nodes.label: Meshech
nodes.description: Meshech is one of the sons listed under Japheth in Genesis 10. This pilot records the genealogical name without adding a modern people-group identification.
nodes.editorial_note: Genealogical presentation in the text; individual/eponym/people interpretation is not resolved.

nodes.label: Tiras
nodes.description: Tiras is one of the sons listed under Japheth in Genesis 10. The passage gives no separate individual story, and this pilot leaves its person or people-group interpretation unresolved.
nodes.editorial_note: Genealogical presentation in the text; individual/eponym/people interpretation is not resolved.

nodes.label: Joktan
nodes.description: Joktan is Eber’s son and Peleg’s brother, with a list of sons of his own in Genesis 10. This entry preserves the genealogical presentation without forcing an individual or people-group interpretation.
nodes.editorial_note: Genealogical presentation in the text; individual/eponym/people interpretation is not resolved.

nodes.label: Hagar
nodes.description: Hagar is Sarah’s Egyptian servant and the mother of Abraham’s son Ishmael. She flees after Sarai treats her harshly, and later is sent away with her son; the narrative describes God opening her eyes to a well.

nodes.label: Ishmael
nodes.description: Ishmael is Abraham’s son by Hagar and the brother who joins Isaac in burying Abraham. Genesis 25 lists twelve sons of Ishmael and calls them princes according to their nations.

nodes.label: Isaac
nodes.description: Isaac is Abraham and Sarah’s son; Abraham binds him for an offering but is stopped before killing him. Isaac marries Rebekah, who gives birth to Esau and Jacob.

nodes.label: Rebekah
nodes.description: Rebekah is Bethuel’s daughter and Laban’s sister; she agrees to leave with Abraham’s servant and becomes Isaac’s wife. She later gives birth to twins, Esau and Jacob.

nodes.label: Bethuel
nodes.description: Bethuel is a son of Milcah and Nahor and the father of Rebekah. He and Laban answer Abraham’s servant concerning Rebekah’s marriage.

nodes.label: Laban
nodes.description: Laban is Bethuel’s son, Rebekah’s brother, and Leah and Rachel’s father. Jacob serves in his household and later leaves with his family; the two men conclude an agreement after Laban overtakes him.

nodes.label: Jacob (Israel)
nodes.description: Jacob, also named Israel, is Isaac and Rebekah’s son and the father of the twelve sons listed in Genesis 35. He marries Leah and Rachel, returns from Laban’s household, and reconciles with Esau.

nodes.label: Esau
nodes.description: Esau is Isaac and Rebekah’s firstborn twin and a skilled hunter. He is also called Edom in the red-stew account, in which he sells his birthright to Jacob.

nodes.label: Keturah
nodes.description: Keturah is named as another wife taken by Abraham. The passage lists six sons she bears him and additional descendants.

nodes.label: Abimelech (Genesis 20–21)
nodes.description: Abimelech, king of Gerar, takes Sarah after Abraham calls her his sister, then restores her. He later makes a covenant with Abraham at Beersheba; no identity with later namesakes is asserted.

nodes.label: Phicol (Genesis 21)
nodes.description: Phicol is the captain of Abimelech’s army who accompanies him when he speaks to Abraham. After the covenant at Beersheba, he returns with Abimelech to the land of the Philistines.

nodes.label: Pharaoh (Genesis 12)
nodes.description: Sarai is taken into the unnamed Pharaoh’s house after his princes praise her beauty. After the plagues, he confronts Abram and sends him away with his wife and possessions.

nodes.label: Melchizedek
nodes.description: Melchizedek is king of Salem and priest of God Most High. He brings bread and wine, blesses Abram, and receives a tenth from him.

nodes.label: Eliezer of Damascus
nodes.description: Abram names Eliezer of Damascus as the person who will inherit his estate while he remains childless. This entry does not identify him with the unnamed servant sent to find Isaac a wife in Genesis 24.

nodes.label: Ephron
nodes.description: Ephron the Hittite, son of Zohar, negotiates with Abraham over a burial place. Abraham pays the named price, and the field and cave become his possession.

nodes.label: Zohar (Ephron’s father)
nodes.description: Zohar is named as Ephron’s father in the burial-place negotiations and again in the account of Abraham’s burial. No additional individual story is given in these passages.

nodes.label: Mamre (Abram’s ally)
nodes.description: Mamre is named as an Amorite and a brother of Eshcol and Aner, allied with Abram. This person is distinguished from the place references to the oaks of Mamre.

nodes.label: Aner
nodes.description: Aner is named with Eshcol and Mamre among Abram’s allies. Abram says these men should receive their share after the recovery of Lot and the goods.

nodes.label: Eshcol (Abram’s ally)
nodes.description: Eshcol is named as Mamre’s brother and one of Abram’s allies. Abram includes him among the men entitled to a share after the recovery of the captives and goods.

nodes.label: Chedorlaomer
nodes.description: Chedorlaomer is king of Elam and part of the four-king coalition opposed by five kings in the valley of Siddim. The account later describes Abram’s return from defeating him and his allied kings.

nodes.label: Bera
nodes.description: Bera is named as king of Sodom among the rulers who fight the four-king coalition. Later unnamed references to the king of Sodom are not automatically assigned to him in the mention layer.

nodes.label: Birsha
nodes.description: Birsha is named as king of Gomorrah among the rulers opposing the four-king coalition. This pilot records the named ruler without resolving every later royal title.

nodes.label: Moab (Lot’s son)
nodes.description: Moab is the son born to Lot’s firstborn daughter after the account of the daughters becoming pregnant by their father. The text calls him the father of the Moabites; the people are not merged with this individual.

nodes.label: Ben Ammi
nodes.description: Ben Ammi is the son born to Lot’s younger daughter after the account of the daughters becoming pregnant by their father. The text calls him the father of the children of Ammon.

nodes.label: Zimran
nodes.description: Zimran is listed among the sons Keturah bears to Abraham. This entry preserves the genealogical presentation without assigning a later people-group identity.

nodes.label: Jokshan
nodes.description: Jokshan is listed among the sons Keturah bears to Abraham. This entry preserves the genealogical presentation without assigning a later people-group identity.

nodes.label: Medan
nodes.description: Medan is listed among the sons Keturah bears to Abraham. This entry preserves the genealogical presentation without assigning a later people-group identity.

nodes.label: Midian
nodes.description: Midian is listed among the sons Keturah bears to Abraham. This entry preserves the genealogical presentation without assigning a later people-group identity.

nodes.label: Ishbak
nodes.description: Ishbak is listed among the sons Keturah bears to Abraham. This entry preserves the genealogical presentation without assigning a later people-group identity.

nodes.label: Shuah
nodes.description: Shuah is listed among the sons Keturah bears to Abraham. This entry preserves the genealogical presentation without assigning a later people-group identity.

nodes.label: Egypt
nodes.description: Egypt is where Abram goes during famine and where Pharaoh takes Sarai into his house. It is also named as the homeland from which Hagar finds a wife for her son.

nodes.label: Shechem (place)
nodes.description: Shechem is a place Abram passes through on entering Canaan, near the oak of Moreh. This is a place entry, not a later individual of the same name.

nodes.label: Oak of Moreh
nodes.description: The oak of Moreh is the landmark named with Shechem in Abram’s journey through Canaan. It is recorded as a textual place without modern coordinates.

nodes.label: Bethel
nodes.description: Bethel is the place west of Abram’s campsite, with Ai to the east. Abram later returns to the area and calls on Yahweh’s name at the altar.

nodes.label: Ai
nodes.description: Ai is named east of Abram’s campsite near Bethel. It helps locate the campsite and altar in the narrative, without a modern identification here.

nodes.label: Plain of the Jordan
nodes.description: The well-watered plain of the Jordan is the area Lot chooses when separating from Abram. He then lives in the cities of the plain and pitches his tent toward Sodom.

nodes.label: Sodom
nodes.description: Sodom is the city associated with Lot’s settlement and captivity. Genesis 19 narrates Lot’s escape and the city’s destruction by sulfur and fire.

nodes.label: Gomorrah
nodes.description: Gomorrah is paired with Sodom in the accounts of the kings’ war and the cities’ destruction. The narrative says Yahweh rains sulfur and fire on both cities.

nodes.label: Zoar / Bela
nodes.description: Bela is identified as Zoar in the account of the kings. Lot escapes to Zoar before leaving it to live in the mountains with his daughters.

nodes.label: Hebron / Kiriath Arba
nodes.description: Hebron is associated with Abram’s dwelling by the oaks of Mamre. Sarah dies there; the text identifies it as Kiriath Arba and locates her burial nearby.

nodes.label: Mamre (place)
nodes.description: The oaks of Mamre are Abram’s dwelling place in Hebron and the setting where Yahweh appears and three men appear. The place entry is distinct from Mamre, Abram’s ally.

nodes.label: Salem
nodes.description: Salem is the place of which Melchizedek is called king. This pilot does not equate it with any other city.

nodes.label: Gerar
nodes.description: Gerar is where Abraham lives as a foreigner and where Abimelech is king. The account there concerns Sarah’s being taken and restored.

nodes.label: Beersheba
nodes.description: Beersheba appears as the wilderness where Hagar wanders and as the place of Abraham and Abimelech’s oath. Abraham later lives there after returning from the testing episode.

nodes.label: Beer Lahai Roi
nodes.description: Beer Lahai Roi is the well named after Hagar’s encounter in the wilderness, located between Kadesh and Bered. Isaac is later described as living by it.

nodes.label: Shur
nodes.description: Shur is named on the route by the fountain where Yahweh’s angel finds Hagar. It is also a boundary reference in Abraham’s travels and the account of Ishmael’s descendants.

nodes.label: Kadesh / En Mishpat
nodes.description: En Mishpat is identified as Kadesh in the account of the kings’ campaign. Kadesh also locates Beer Lahai Roi and the area where Abraham later lives.

nodes.label: Wilderness of Paran
nodes.description: The wilderness of Paran is where Hagar’s son lives after the account of water being provided. His mother obtains a wife for him from Egypt.

nodes.label: Land of Moriah
nodes.description: Moriah is the land named in God’s command to Abraham concerning Isaac’s offering. This pilot does not identify the mountain with a later sanctuary or modern site.

nodes.label: Machpelah
nodes.description: Machpelah is the named burial property whose field and cave Abraham acquires. Sarah is buried in its cave, and Isaac and Ishmael later bury Abraham there beside her.

nodes.label: Mesopotamia
nodes.description: Mesopotamia is the region to which Abraham’s servant travels, reaching the city of Nahor. This pilot does not identify that city with Haran or resolve its name as a person mention.

nodes.label: Paddan Aram
nodes.description: Paddan Aram is named in the description of Bethuel, Rebekah’s father. This pilot retains the place name without assigning modern boundaries.

nodes.label: Elam (kingdom)
nodes.description: Elam is the kingdom whose ruler is named as Chedorlaomer in the four-king coalition. This place is not merged with genealogical names or modern states.

nodes.label: Leah
nodes.description: Leah is Laban’s elder daughter and one of Jacob’s wives. She is named as the mother of six sons and Dinah in the family narrative.

nodes.label: Rachel
nodes.description: Rachel is Laban’s younger daughter, Jacob’s wife, and the mother of Joseph and Benjamin. She dies during Benjamin’s birth and is buried on the way to Ephrath.

nodes.label: Bilhah
nodes.description: Bilhah is given to Rachel as a servant and later to Jacob as a wife. She bears Dan and Naphtali; Genesis 35 also describes her as Jacob’s concubine.

nodes.label: Zilpah
nodes.description: Zilpah is given to Leah as a servant and later to Jacob as a wife. She bears Gad and Asher in the family narrative.

nodes.label: Reuben
nodes.description: Reuben is Jacob’s firstborn son and Leah’s son. He brings mandrakes to Leah, and a later passage recounts his lying with Bilhah, his father’s concubine.

nodes.label: Simeon
nodes.description: Simeon is one of Jacob and Leah’s sons and Dinah’s brother. He and Levi attack the city after Dinah’s violation and kill Hamor and Shechem.

nodes.label: Levi
nodes.description: Levi is one of Jacob and Leah’s sons and Dinah’s brother. He and Simeon attack the city and kill Hamor and Shechem after the account of Dinah’s violation.

nodes.label: Judah
nodes.description: Judah is Jacob and Leah’s son, who proposes selling Joseph and later offers to remain in Egypt in Benjamin’s place. His family story includes Tamar and their twins Perez and Zerah.

nodes.label: Dan (Jacob’s son)
nodes.description: Dan is the son Bilhah bears to Jacob and Rachel names. This individual is not merged with the place called Dan in the earlier account of Abram’s pursuit.

nodes.label: Naphtali
nodes.description: Naphtali is Bilhah’s second son by Jacob, named by Rachel. He appears again in the list of Jacob’s sons.

nodes.label: Gad
nodes.description: Gad is the first son named after Zilpah is given to Jacob as a wife. Leah names him, and Genesis 35 lists him among Zilpah’s sons.

nodes.label: Asher
nodes.description: Asher is Zilpah’s second son by Jacob, named by Leah. He is later listed with Gad among Zilpah’s sons.

nodes.label: Issachar
nodes.description: Issachar is the fifth son Leah bears to Jacob. He is listed among Leah’s sons in the later family summary.

nodes.label: Zebulun
nodes.description: Zebulun is the sixth son Leah bears to Jacob. His birth is followed by the notice of Dinah’s birth.

nodes.label: Dinah
nodes.description: Dinah is the daughter of Leah and Jacob. Genesis 34 recounts Shechem’s violation of her and the subsequent violence by her brothers Simeon and Levi.

nodes.label: Joseph
nodes.description: Joseph, son of Jacob and Rachel, is sold into Egypt, serves in Potiphar’s house and later interprets Pharaoh’s dreams. Pharaoh puts him over Egypt, and Joseph supplies food for his family during the famine before dying there.

nodes.label: Benjamin
nodes.description: Benjamin is Jacob and Rachel’s younger son and Joseph’s brother. He accompanies the brothers to Egypt, where Joseph recognizes him and later reveals himself to the family.

nodes.label: Hamor
nodes.description: Hamor is Shechem’s father, who negotiates with Jacob’s family after the violation of Dinah. Simeon and Levi kill him and his son in the attack on the city.

nodes.label: Shechem (Hamor’s son)
nodes.description: Shechem, Hamor’s son, violates Dinah and seeks to marry her. He and Hamor are killed by Simeon and Levi; this person is distinct from the city named Shechem.

nodes.label: Deborah (Rebekah’s nurse)
nodes.description: Deborah is named as Rebekah’s nurse. Her death and burial below Bethel under the oak are recorded during Jacob’s return.

nodes.label: Abimelech (Genesis 26)
nodes.description: Abimelech is the king of the Philistines whom Isaac encounters at Gerar. He later visits Isaac with Ahuzzath and Phicol, and the parties swear an oath before parting in peace.

nodes.label: Phicol (Genesis 26)
nodes.description: Phicol is the captain of Abimelech’s army in the account of his visit to Isaac. This entry does not assert that he is the same person as the Phicol in Abraham’s earlier story.

nodes.label: Ahuzzath
nodes.description: Ahuzzath is named as Abimelech’s friend when he accompanies the king and Phicol to Isaac. No further individual story is given in this passage.

nodes.label: Esek (well)
nodes.description: Esek is the well Isaac names after the dispute between the herdsmen of Gerar and his own herdsmen. Its name is linked in the narrative to contention.

nodes.label: Sitnah (well)
nodes.description: Sitnah is the name given to another well over which the herdsmen argue. The narrative places it between the disputes at Esek and the move to Rehoboth.

nodes.label: Rehoboth (well)
nodes.description: Rehoboth is the well Isaac names where there is no dispute. This well is not automatically identified with the other place names containing Rehoboth in Genesis.

nodes.label: Mountain of Gilead
nodes.description: The mountain of Gilead is where Laban overtakes Jacob after Jacob’s departure. Both households encamp there during their confrontation.

nodes.label: Galeed / Jegar Sahadutha
nodes.description: Galeed is Jacob’s name for the heap of stones set up during his agreement with Laban; Laban calls it Jegar Sahadutha. The passage also associates it with the name Mizpah.

nodes.label: Mahanaim
nodes.description: Mahanaim is the name Jacob gives the place where angels of God meet him. No modern geographic identification is added.

nodes.label: Seir (hill country)
nodes.description: Seir is the hill country associated with Esau’s residence. This place is distinguished from Seir the Horite in the genealogy.

nodes.label: Edom (land)
nodes.description: Edom is a territorial name in the account of Esau’s descendants and rulers. It is kept separate from explicit personal uses of Edom as Esau’s alternate name.

nodes.label: Jabbok
nodes.description: The Jabbok is the stream whose ford Jacob crosses with his family before the wrestling episode. The narrative does not give a modern coordinate.

nodes.label: Peniel
nodes.description: Peniel is the place Jacob names after the wrestling encounter, explaining that he has seen God face to face. The name is recorded without resolving the wrestler’s identity.

nodes.label: Succoth (place)
nodes.description: Succoth is where Jacob builds a house and shelters for his livestock after parting from Esau. The narrative connects the name with those shelters.

nodes.label: Ephrath / Bethlehem
nodes.description: Ephrath, also called Bethlehem, is named along the route where Rachel dies and is buried. The text says her burial is on the way to the place, not necessarily inside the town.

nodes.label: Allon Bacuth
nodes.description: Allon Bacuth is the name given to the oak below Bethel where Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, is buried. It is recorded as a textual burial landmark.

nodes.label: Potiphar
nodes.description: Potiphar is Pharaoh’s officer and captain of the guard who buys Joseph in Egypt and makes him overseer of his household. He is not merged with Potiphera, the priest of On named later.

nodes.label: Potiphar’s wife (unnamed)
nodes.description: Potiphar’s unnamed wife repeatedly asks Joseph to lie with her; after he refuses and runs away, she accuses him before her household and husband. The accusation is reported as her speech, not adopted as a fact about Joseph.
nodes.editorial_note: Unnamed role-scoped person, not given a traditional personal name. Only two explicit role-phrase mentions are annotated; pronouns omitted.

nodes.label: Pharaoh (Joseph narrative)
nodes.description: The unnamed Pharaoh of the Joseph narrative summons Joseph to interpret dreams and places him over Egypt. He welcomes Joseph’s family and later permits Joseph to bury his father in Canaan.
nodes.editorial_note: Narrative-role continuity within Genesis37–50; not a historical identification of a particular monarch or a claim about reign chronology. Separate from Pharaoh in Genesis12.

nodes.label: Chief cup bearer (Joseph narrative)
nodes.description: Pharaoh’s chief cup bearer is imprisoned with Joseph, who interprets his dream. He is restored to office, initially forgets Joseph, and later tells Pharaoh about him.
nodes.editorial_note: Unnamed official; scoped title mentions only.

nodes.label: Chief baker (Joseph narrative)
nodes.description: Pharaoh’s chief baker is imprisoned with Joseph and tells him a dream. Joseph predicts his death, and the narrative later reports that Pharaoh hangs him.
nodes.editorial_note: Unnamed official; scoped title mentions only. Prediction and narrated outcome are distinguished.

nodes.label: Asenath
nodes.description: Asenath, daughter of Potiphera the priest of On, is given to Joseph as his wife. She bears him Manasseh and Ephraim before the famine.

nodes.label: Potiphera
nodes.description: Potiphera is the priest of On and Asenath’s father. His name is kept distinct from Potiphar, the officer who buys Joseph.

nodes.label: Manasseh
nodes.description: Manasseh is Joseph and Asenath’s firstborn son. When Jacob blesses the two brothers, he places his left hand on Manasseh and gives the younger Ephraim precedence.
nodes.editorial_note: Individual son in these scenes; no automatic merging with later tribe or territory.

nodes.label: Ephraim
nodes.description: Ephraim is Joseph and Asenath’s younger son. Jacob crosses his hands to place his right hand on Ephraim and puts him before Manasseh in his blessing.
nodes.editorial_note: Individual son in these scenes; future people-group predictions remain attributed to Jacob.

nodes.label: Machir (Manasseh’s son)
nodes.description: Machir is identified as Manasseh’s son in the closing account of Joseph’s life. The narrative says that Machir’s children were born on Joseph’s knees.
nodes.editorial_note: No further adoption, parentage, or later tribal identity is inferred from the idiom.

nodes.label: Hirah
nodes.description: Hirah is the Adullamite whom Judah visits and later accompanies to the sheep shearers. He is called Judah’s friend and is sent with the promised goat to find the woman Judah had met.

nodes.label: Shua (Judah’s father-in-law)
nodes.description: Shua is the Canaanite man whose unnamed daughter becomes Judah’s wife. The narrative later reports the daughter’s death, without giving her a personal name.

nodes.label: Shua’s daughter (unnamed)
nodes.description: Shua’s unnamed daughter becomes Judah’s wife and bears Er, Onan and Shelah. She later dies, and Judah travels with Hirah after his mourning.
nodes.editorial_note: No traditional personal name is assigned; only an explicit role phrase is annotated.

nodes.label: Er (Judah’s son)
nodes.description: Er is Judah’s firstborn son and Tamar’s husband. The narrative says that he was wicked in Yahweh’s sight and that Yahweh killed him.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual attribution, not independent moral or historical verification.

nodes.label: Onan
nodes.description: Onan is Judah’s son and Er’s brother. After Judah tells him to provide offspring for his brother through Tamar, he refuses to provide that offspring; the narrative reports his death as Yahweh’s action.

nodes.label: Shelah (Judah’s son)
nodes.description: Shelah is Judah’s son whom Tamar is told to wait for after Er and Onan die. Although he grows up, she is not given to him as a wife; he is distinct from Shelah in the earlier genealogy through Eber.

nodes.label: Tamar
nodes.description: Tamar is Er’s wife and Judah’s daughter-in-law. After being withheld from Shelah, she conceives by Judah and gives birth to twins, Perez and Zerah.

nodes.label: Perez
nodes.description: Perez is one of Tamar’s twins by Judah and the brother of Zerah. Genesis 46 names Hezron and Hamul as his sons.

nodes.label: Zerah (Tamar’s son)
nodes.description: Zerah is Tamar’s son by Judah and Perez’s twin brother, identified in the birth account by the scarlet thread on his hand. He is kept separate from the Zerah in Esau’s family list.

nodes.label: Dothan
nodes.description: Dothan is where Joseph finds his brothers after looking for them at Shechem. The account of their plot against him follows his arrival there.

nodes.label: Timnah (Judah narrative)
nodes.description: Timnah is where Judah goes with Hirah to his sheep shearers after his wife’s death. Tamar learns he is going there and waits by the road at Enaim.
nodes.editorial_note: Not merged with people named Timna in genealogies; no modern-site identification.

nodes.label: Enaim
nodes.description: Enaim is the place on the road to Timnah where Tamar waits with her face covered. Hirah later asks there about the woman Judah had met.

nodes.label: On
nodes.description: On is the place associated with Potiphera’s priesthood in the notices naming Asenath as Joseph’s wife and their sons’ mother. No modern identification is assigned here.

nodes.label: Goshen
nodes.description: Goshen is the area in Egypt where Joseph meets his father and where the family settles during the famine. Their children and livestock remain there when the burial party goes to Canaan.

nodes.label: Land of Rameses
nodes.description: The land of Rameses is the area where Joseph gives his father and brothers a possession, described as part of the best land of Egypt. It is not automatically equated with Goshen or a later named city.

nodes.label: Threshing floor of Atad / Abel Mizraim
nodes.description: The funeral party for Jacob mourns at the threshing floor of Atad beyond the Jordan. The account says the place is called Abel Mizraim because of the mourning observed there.
nodes.editorial_note: Atad is treated as part of a place designation, not an independently identified person.

nodes.label: Garden in Eden
nodes.description: The garden planted by Yahweh God in Eden is where the man is placed. The account names the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil among its trees.
nodes.editorial_note: Textual garden, distinguished from the wider named region Eden; no modern geography.

nodes.label: River flowing out of Eden
nodes.description: An unnamed river flows out of Eden to water the garden and divides into the source of four named rivers. Its identity is retained as the narrative describes it, without a modern river reconstruction.
nodes.editorial_note: Anonymous textual river; not equated with one of its four named branches or a modern river.

nodes.label: Abraham’s unnamed servant (Genesis 24)
nodes.description: Abraham sends his unnamed senior household servant to his relatives to find a wife for Isaac. The servant travels to Mesopotamia and returns with Rebekah; the text does not name him Eliezer.
nodes.editorial_note: Role-labeled person scoped to this mission; no identity with Eliezer asserted. Literal role mentions are narrowly scoped and exclude “your servant Isaac” in 24:14.

Narrator describes God placing cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the way to the tree. The edge records arranging guards, not God acting as the individual guard or an identity for the cherubim.

Jacob is the explicitly identified father among the family Joseph settles in Rameses. This contextual individual participation does not equate Rameses with Goshen or a later city.
Joseph is explicitly named as leading/participating in the funeral party that arrives at Atad; this is a shared journey, not an assertion that he traveled alone.

Hamor goes to Jacob to discuss the proposed marriage; this does not assert that the marriage took place or assign individual agents to the later joint killings.
